newsitem.title: UK: World LPG surges on Saudi term price, low US stock.
newsitem.headline: World LPG surges on Saudi term price, low US stock.

text.p: World liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices pushed higher this week supported by expectations of a sharp rise in Saudi term contract prices for December and recent heavy draws on U.S. stocks.
Despite high stocks and sluggish end-user buying interest, European spot prices made strong gains, dragged up by surging U.S. and Middle Eastern markets.
"It's the other markets that are strong, not Europe...Germany isn't buying beyond contract requirements as storage is pretty much full," said one European trader.
Nevertheless, on Thursday, a propane coaster traded early at $310 a tonne fob Teeside, while another traded later out of the ARA region at $350, some $70 a tonne up on last week's levels.

The large ships propane market in Europe was also stronger, with a cargo traded into France at $330 cif Le Havre, for first-half December delivery. But butane was thinly talked with cargoes valued fairly steady at $260/$270 cif NWE.
Across the Atlantic, propane prices leapt by some 14 percent over the week to 65 cents a gallon (around $330 a tonne) at the major trading hub at Mont Belvieu, Texas.
Average November U.S. propane prices are expected to average 55 cents a gallon, about 75 percent above the four year historical average of 31.40 cents.
Cold weather, particularly in the northeastern states, forced a 1.3 million draw on already-depleted LPG inventories last week, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) said.

Adding to the upward pressure were predictions that there will be few import cargoes to the U.S. over the next few months as prices of exports from dominant supplier Saudi Arabia shoot through the roof.

Saudi Aramco's T3 tender was bid on Friday with the final price expected to top $300 after the T1 tender for early December delivery was awarded at a bullish $293 a tonne for propane and around $297 for butane. The T2 tender was cancelled.
On this basis, the December contract price (CP) is widely expected to reach $300 a tonne.
"Certainly it'll be over $300, it could be as high as $330, depending on how desperate they perceive the market to be," said one trader.
Middle East fob premiums were steady at around CP+$25 for propane and CP+$35 for butane.
In the Far east, propane was offered at CP+$65 c+f Japan, with bids no higher than the mid-50s.
"It's a very expensive market. The main buyers are trying to hold off," said a trader for an international major.
Japanese importers said earlier in the week that they intend to spot buying spot cargoes if the December CP breaks the $300 mark.
"If they don't get cold weather they could just about muddle through," a trader said.
Another option is to draw supplies from mandatory stockpiles if a sharp rise in import prices seriously squeezes domestic supplies, A senior Energy Agency official said on Thursday.
